title: Evidence Extraction Tables

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are structured summaries that pull key claims, study designs, populations, interventions, outcomes, and effect sizes from primary research into a comparable grid. They sit within literature review and evidence synthesis, where a reviewer needs to see many studies side by side without rereading full texts. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10,767 extracted claims reflects the volume such tables are built to manage. They are not literature search tools; they are a downstream artifact for appraisal and synthesis.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These tables are usually built in spreadsheet software, reference managers, or dedicated systematic review platforms, and they can be stored as CSV, JSON, or database rows. On this site, the underlying data is drawn from the paper library and claim store, and links always point to the original paper rather than to any third party search tool. The infrastructure is deliberately simple: a table schema, a source identifier, and a claim record that can be filtered and exported.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by reading each included study and recording predefined fields, often with two reviewers working independently and then reconciling differences. Extraction is guided by a protocol or codebook so that every row answers the same question in the same way. For AI related evidence, the table may capture model type, training data, evaluation metric, and reported performance, but the core method remains manual, structured, and auditable.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on accuracy, provenance, and version control. Every extracted claim must trace back to a specific passage in the original paper, and the site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool supports that traceability. Risks include transcription error, selective extraction, and outdated rows when a paper is corrected or retracted, so tables need clear ownership and a change log. No table entry should be treated as legal, financial, investment, or medical advice; it is a record of what a source reported.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are moving toward semiautomated population from full text using language models, with human review remaining for disputed or high stakes fields. The site's catalogue of 803 scientific models and 732 AI tools suggests the surrounding ecosystem is large enough to support such automation, but the table itself will likely stay a human governed artifact. Future versions may include live links to retraction notices, registered protocols, and machine readable claim identifiers that make synthesis faster without weakening provenance.
